quote: It is furthermore claimed that if zombies are “possible” (a term over which battles are still being fought), then, purely from our knowledge of this “possibility,” we can deduce a priori that consciousness is extra-physical, in a sense to be described below; the standard term for this position is “epiphenomenalism.”
content: The conclusion of the zombie argument is that physicalism is false; epiphenomenalism is one of three positions Chalmers lists as compatible with that conclusion (The Conscious Mind, ch. 4), the others being interactionism and a Russellian or panprotopsychist monism, and it is the third that he has since described as the most promising (“Panpsychism and Panprotopsychism,” 2013). Of epiphenomenalism he wrote that it was “a natural but not inevitable” consequence and that he was “not especially attached” to it, and his reason for not embracing interactionism was the empirical case for the causal closure of physics, which he has since treated as an open question that quantum collapse theories might reopen (Chalmers & McQueen (2022)). So the essay’s “why, oh why, say that the extra properties are epiphenomenal?” has an answer in the book it is attacking: because of a premise about physics, held tentatively, with the causal alternative explicitly on the table. The 6,600 words that follow refute a position their target holds provisionally and has partly abandoned, and leave untouched the version, Russellian monism, on which the phenomenal properties are the intrinsic nature of the physical ones and do all the causal work. The essay’s further claim that the possibility of zombies is accepted by “possibly a majority” of philosophers of consciousness is false on the survey evidence: in the 2009 PhilPapers survey, 23% of respondents held zombies metaphysically possible, 36% held them conceivable but not possible, and 16% inconceivable (Bourget & Chalmers (2014)). The plurality position is the one the essay presents as its own discovery.

quote: Because native Chinese speakers can remember longer digit sequences than English-speakers. Chinese digits are all single syllables, and so Chinese speakers can remember around ten digits, versus the famous “seven plus or minus two” for English speakers. There appears to be a loop of repeating sounds back to yourself, a size limit on working memory in the auditory cortex, which is genuinely phoneme-based.
content: The digit-span finding is real (Stigler, Lee & Stevenson (1986)) and it is standard evidence for Baddeley’s phonological loop; that part is fine. The inference to “the sound of these words is probably represented in your auditory cortex, as though you’d heard someone else say it” is not what the neuroscience of inner speech found. Inner speech recruits the left inferior frontal gyrus and premotor areas at least as reliably as auditory cortex, and the review literature treats it as a motor-based simulation with sensory consequences rather than an auditory percept (Alderson-Day & Fernyhough (2015)); more to the point, the auditory response to one’s own inner speech is suppressed relative to hearing someone else, by the same corollary-discharge mechanism that dampens the sound of one’s own voice (Whitford et al. (2017)), so “as though you’d heard someone else say it” is the specific thing the brain arranges not to happen. The prediction that neural taps could read out the narrative has fared better: attempted speech has been decoded from sensorimotor cortex (Anumanchipalli et al. (2019)) and continuous language from fMRI (Tang et al. (2023)), from areas that are not the auditory cortex.

quote: So just because you don’t see a contradiction in the Zombie World at first glance, it doesn’t mean that no contradiction is there. It’s like not seeing a contradiction in the Riemann Hypothesis at first glance.
content: This is the distinction between prima facie and ideal conceivability, and it is Chalmers’s (“Does Conceivability Entail Possibility?”, 2002). The zombie argument in its considered form claims that zombies are ideally conceivable, conceivable on ideal rational reflection with no contradiction to be found by any amount of a priori reasoning, and Chalmers agrees in print that “I don’t see a contradiction yet” establishes nothing. Richard Chappell’s comment quoted in the next essay makes this point and the next essay concedes it while insisting on different words. So the 3-SAT paragraph, correct as computer science, is aimed at a position its target rejected six years earlier. What the essay needs, and what the Riemann analogy invites, is to exhibit the contradiction. Zombie Responses attempts that, and the annotation there records what the attempt assumes. The Riemann Hypothesis is also an awkward comparison for the essay’s side: mathematicians’ inability to find a contradiction in it after 150 years is treated by them as evidence that it is true, and the analogous inference about zombies is the one the essay wants to block.

quote: If you can close your eyes, and sense yourself sensing—if you can be aware of yourself being aware, and think “I am aware that I am aware”—and say out loud, “I am aware that I am aware”—then your consciousness is not without effect on your internal narrative, or your moving lips.
content: This begs the question against the position it is meant to refute. The epiphenomenalist holds that awareness has a physical correlate, that the correlate causes the report, and that awareness accompanies the correlate by a psychophysical law; on that view the sequence the essay describes, focusing followed by a report of focusing, is exactly what is predicted, because the physical correlate of focusing precedes and causes the physical report. “The listener caught in the act of listening” is, to the epiphenomenalist, the correlate caught in the act, and the essay has assumed that the correlate is not what is doing the work. That is the disagreement, restated as an observation. The essay half-knows this, since it immediately grants that “you can argue clever reasons why this is not so,” and the paradox it goes on to press, that the zombie twin writes the same papers, is one Chalmers raised against himself under the name “the paradox of phenomenal judgment” (The Conscious Mind, ch. 5), which is why the essay can quote his statement of it. Whether the paradox is fatal turns on the epistemology of introspection, addressed in the annotation below; it is not settled by saying “I am aware that I am aware” out loud.

quote: Sir Roger Penrose (physicist) and Stuart Hameroff (neurologist) are substance dualists; they think that there is something mysterious going on in quantum, that Everett is wrong and that the “collapse of the wavefunction” is physically real, and that this is where consciousness lives
content: Penrose and Hameroff are not substance dualists; Orchestrated Objective Reduction is a physicalist theory on which consciousness is a physical process, gravitationally induced collapse in neuronal microtubules. Penrose sets out four positions in Shadows of the Mind (1994, §1.3), from strong AI to mysticism, and places himself at C: awareness arises from physical action that current physics does not yet describe. He rejects dualism explicitly. Hameroff is an anaesthesiologist, not a neurologist. The empirical situation is as the essay says: Tegmark’s decoherence calculation put the relevant timescales ten orders of magnitude too short (Tegmark (2000)), Hameroff’s group disputed the parameters (Hagan, Hameroff & Tuszynski (2002)), and the theory remains a minority view without positive evidence. The essay’s praise of Penrose for making a testable proposal is fair. The labels are not, and they matter for the essay’s taxonomy, which sorts the field into reductionists, substance dualists and epiphenomenalists and then finds the third group uniquely deranged; the theory it files under substance dualism is the one that says consciousness is physics.

quote: So—if I’ve got this thesis right—there’s a core you, above and beyond your brain, that believes it is not a zombie, and directly experiences not being a zombie; and so its beliefs are justified.
content: What the essay has got hold of is the acquaintance theory of introspective justification, and it is not a dualist eccentricity. The view that one’s beliefs about one’s current experiences are justified by the experiences themselves rather than by a reliable causal process goes back to Russell’s knowledge by acquaintance (1910) and is held by philosophers of every metaphysical stripe (Gertler (2001); BonJour; Fumerton), including physicalists who think it explains why phenomenal concepts resist functional analysis. The essay’s counter-argument, the reflectively coherent AI that flags any belief-producing process not causally connected to its truth-maker as a bug, assumes process reliabilism, one theory of justification among several, and the annotation on Righting a Wrong Question noted its cost: on that theory, beliefs about mathematics and about the laws of probability are bugs too, since nothing in the causal environment corresponds to them. The essay would have to choose between its reliabilism and its Platonism about theorems. It is also worth saying that the reflective-coherence requirement was later found, by its author, to be unsatisfiable as stated: the Tiling Agents report the next essay cites (Yudkowsky & Herreshoff, 2013, an unpublished technical report) is about the Löbian obstacle, the fact that a consistent agent cannot prove its own soundness. An agent that could inspect its own belief-forming parts and certify them reliable in the way the essay demands would be inconsistent by Löb’s theorem. “Deranged” is a strong word for an epistemology whose rival could not be built.
